newsitem.title: USA: USDA to ask Congress for new enforcement powers.
newsitem.headline: USDA to ask Congress for new enforcement powers.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Wednesday the department would ask Congress for more enforcement powers as part of its efforts to address concentration in the livestock industry.
"By giving the department these additional enforcement tools...I think will help to ensure that farmers are not subject to unfair trade practices in today's marketplace," Glickman told reporters.
He also said USDA would reorganize its antitrust division to better enable it to probe anticompetitive practices.
USDA will ask Congress to provide it with administrative enforcement authority for violations by dealers in live poultry, as it currently has for beef and pork.
Currently, USDA must take its data to the Justice Department and persuade Justice to file a case.

USDA is also seeking authority impose civil penalties and take other steps to administratively enforce the Agricultural Fair Practices Act, which guarantees farmers a fair price regardless of whether they belong to a producer association.
Asked by reporters if he thought Congress would approve USDA's request for more enforcement power, Glickman said, "I think so. I think that they will give us that authority."

The secretary also announced USDA would restructure the Grain Inspection, Packers and Stockyards Administration (GIPSA) and hire 30 more employees to make it more effective in investigating anticompetitive practices.

He said the overhaul was in response to a recent government study that found GIPSA was ill-organized to investigate anti-competitive activities and suggested transferring the antitrust division's responsibilities for such probes to another federal agency such as the Justice Department.

Glickman called on Congress to fund USDA's fiscal year 1998 GIPSA budget request, which includes an additional $1.65 million for increased legal, economic and statistical expertise to purse anticompetitive investigations and $750,000 for investigation and enforcement activities in the poultry area. Finally, Glickman said USDA would work to help
livestock producers use new market information reports the department began releasing last Fall.
Wednesday's aannouncements were the latest in a series of actions taken by the department to address concentration in the livestock industry.

Chuck Lambert, chief economist for the National Cattlemen's Beef Association said the proposed changes were significant because they would streamline enforcement of the two laws. "This will allow USDA to bring these cases directly," he said.
